why: A working simulator of a 36-bit Honeywell mainframe lets you boot and poke at a machine architecture almost nobody has touched.

brief.what_it_is: DPS8M is an open source simulator of the 36-bit GE Large Systems / Honeywell / Bull 600/6000-series mainframe computers, specifically the Honeywell 6180, Honeywell Series-60 / Level-68, and Honeywell / Bull DPS-8/M. It runs on a host computer and emulates that machine, so software written for the hardware can run on it. The homepage names the executables as dps8, prt2pdf, punutil and tap2raw, taken from the package metadata rather than from any README text I read. I could not read a usage section, so I cannot say what inputs they expect or what they print.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says the machines are descended from the GE-645 and were engineered to support the Multics operating system, which is the reason this simulator targets that lineage.
brief.install_notes: Nothing beyond the brew formula was visible to me. The brew metadata lists four executables (dps8, prt2pdf, punutil, tap2raw) but I found no build steps, runtime requirements, configuration, or first-run instructions. The GitLab README I reached only pointed to the project wiki, so those details are probably there.
brief.standout: A working emulator of a 36-bit Honeywell mainframe is rare, and the brew-supplied scout note suggests it can boot and be explored. That claim comes from the scout note and I did not verify it in the README. The homepage also says a hardware DPS-8/M and FNP project on FPGA was underway as of 2024.
brief.status: Maintained, with evidence from the homepage. The latest release listed is R3.1.0 (2025-05-14), with earlier releases 3.0.1 (2023-08-10) and 3.0.0 (2022-11-23). The GitLab project page shows it was created on February 02, 2019. I did not find a last-commit date.
brief.caveats: The README I could read was thin: the GitLab repository page and the README stub both pointed to the wiki instead of giving content. The documentation URL I guessed returned HTTP 404, so I could not check the docs. I found no license text, platform list, or build instructions. The brew caveats field was empty.

entry.title: DPS8M
entry.tldr: A simulator of the 36-bit Honeywell/GE mainframes built to run Multics, so you can run software for hardware almost nobody has touched.
entry.deeper_look:
DPS8M simulates the 36-bit GE Large Systems / Honeywell / Bull 600/6000-series mainframes. Specifically it covers the Honeywell 6180, the Series-60 / Level-68, and the DPS-8/M. It runs on an ordinary host machine and emulates the hardware, so software written for those mainframes can run on it.

The reason this lineage matters is Multics. The homepage says these machines are "descended from the GE-645 and engineered to support the Multics operating system." The simulator exists to keep that family of machines runnable, long after the physical hardware went out of service.

The formula installs four executables: `dps8`, the simulator itself, plus `prt2pdf`, `punutil` and `tap2raw`. The names suggest helpers for printer output, punched cards and tape images, which fits the era. The brief did not include usage details for them, so treat that as a guess from the names.

The idea underneath is a machine with 36-bit words, from before the 8-bit byte became universal. Running it shows you a different architecture that you can actually use, not just read about. The homepage also mentions a hardware DPS-8/M and FNP project on FPGA, underway as of 2024.
